title: Pepsi-Cola Bottling Company of Pittsburg, Inc. v. PepsiCo, Inc.
lead: An independent Pepsi distributor could demand reasonable protection of its own territory, but could not enforce a competing bottler’s agreement merely because it benefited from that agreement.

actors.name: Bottling Group
actors.role: Anchor bottler and alleged source of transshipped products

actors.name: Southeast Kansas Vending
actors.role: Reseller whose dealings supported a surviving interference claim

proceedings: District court: summary judgment for defendants on all claims; Rule 59(e) motion denied.
Tenth Circuit: reversed on PepsiCo’s reasonable territorial-protection duty and Bottling Group’s SEK interference claim; otherwise affirmed and remanded.
limits: The December 20, 2005 decision differs from the assigned 2006 date. No damages or final liability was established. Beneficiary, direct-contract, and interference theories received different dispositions.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The bottler accepts exclusivity with its own commercial obligations
sections.cue: Introduce the original appointment and the later distribution changes.
paragraphs: In September 1959, Pepsi-Cola Bottling Company of Pittsburg, called Pittsburg Pepsi, received an Exclusive Bottling Appointment for designated Kansas and Missouri territory. PepsiCo supplied concentrate and controlled trademarks. Pittsburg Pepsi promised not to distribute competing cola, to buy its concentrate requirements, and to market vigorously using its own resources. It set resale prices and bore advertising expenses. The agreement required signed written amendments, preserved rights against waiver, and chose New York law. Later appointments separately covered other beverages and their competing flavor categories. By the dispute, Pittsburg Pepsi bought manufactured products through a bottler cooperative rather than operating a plant.

PepsiCo publicly emphasized perpetual territorial exclusivity and in 1984 created a transshipment enforcement program. Transshipment meant another bottler’s product appearing in someone else’s assigned territory. PepsiCo could investigate and impose charges payable to the invaded bottler.

National chains later sought unified purchasing, and Coca-Cola’s consolidation increased pressure to align the Pepsi system. PepsiCo used customer development agreements with retailers and marketplace investment agreements with bottlers to share rebates and advertising. Pittsburg Pepsi declined the latter, avoiding contributions but receiving no associated marketing money; PepsiCo still paid the retailer-agreement costs in its territory.

sections.title: An anchor bottler and outside resellers test the territorial arrangement
sections.cue: Keep the separate customers and alleged strategy distinct.
paragraphs: In 1999, PepsiCo established anchor bottlers, including Bottling Group, whose master agreement covered parts of forty-one states. Internal materials identified unaligned bottlers and proposed withholding support or new appointments. Pittsburg Pepsi alleged a plan to weaken independents for acquisition; the court later considered favorable inferences at summary judgment without finding that purpose proved.

Grace Energy, a multiterritory convenience-store operator, received Bottling Group offers allegedly suggesting authority to speak for Pittsburg Pepsi. Southeast Kansas Vending, or SEK, bought most Pepsi products through a Sam’s Club supplied by Bottling Group and resold within Pittsburg Pepsi’s territory. Repeated complaints met denials of knowledge or requests for source information. Sam’s Club eventually told SEK it could not buy for that resale. Smith Foods Vending separately left Pittsburg Pepsi over prices and stocked territorial machines with Bottling Group products; a Bottling Group representative later told it to stop transshipping.

After an initial dismissal motion failed, Pittsburg Pepsi’s six-count amended complaint asserted contract, fiduciary, beneficiary, interference, conspiracy, and restraint-of-trade theories. The district court granted defense summary judgment on all claims and denied a Rule 59(e) motion. On de novo review, Kansas choice-of-law rules led to New York contract and beneficiary law and Kansas tort law. The appointments chiefly governed goods sales and fell under the Uniform Commercial Code despite incidental services. Pittsburg Pepsi abandoned restraint-of-trade and aiding-and-abetting claims.

sections.title: Past appointments and good faith do not promise every future benefit
paragraphs: Pittsburg Pepsi claimed nearly forty years of new-product appointments modified its original agreement or established an implied promise of all future products. Judge Briscoe, writing for Judges Henry and Hartz as well, rejected both. No signed writing satisfied the amendment requirement, and successive product agreements were separate bargains rather than a course of altered performance under one contract. An implied agreement could not add terms on a subject already governed expressly. The appellate court used that reasoning rather than the district court’s consideration rationale.

The dispute remained live despite PepsiCo’s later offer and Pittsburg Pepsi’s acceptance of the appointments: twenty-one months of withholding could still have caused damages. But good faith could not supply a right to all future products. It also could not require advertising payments contrary to Pittsburg Pepsi’s express duty to advertise at its own expense. The only identified fund source was the investment agreement it declined. The covenant protected existing benefits rather than creating inconsistent new ones.

sections.title: Express territorial exclusivity does require reasonable protection
sections.cue: Explain why this contract claim survives without guaranteeing zero encroachment.
paragraphs: Territory differed because exclusivity was a bargained-for benefit. Contract language, conduct, PepsiCo’s public explanations, and good faith required reasonable steps against other bottlers’ encroachment. The court did not make the enforcement program itself an express term or guarantee that transshipment could never occur. Failure to use it together with failure to take other protective measures could show breach of the broader duty.

An employee named Lawrence simultaneously handled PepsiCo franchise development and transshipment enforcement and Bottling Group acquisition efforts. Strategies could encourage territorial customers to buy discounted products outside the area. Pittsburg Pepsi repeatedly complained, while PepsiCo’s response and training remained unclear. A jury could infer knowing tolerance of encroachment to weaken a franchise sought for acquisition. That permissible inference required trial, not a present finding of bad faith. The corresponding covenant theory remained part of this direct contract claim against PepsiCo.

sections.title: The neighboring bottler’s agreement supplies a benefit without a right to enforce
sections.cue: Distinguish third-party status from the surviving direct promise.
paragraphs: Pittsburg Pepsi separately tried to enforce Bottling Group’s master agreement and predecessor exclusive appointments. Under the New York beneficiary tests discussed in Piccoli, PepsiCo itself could enforce those promises. The master agreement added transshipment charges to other remedies; the exclusive appointment retained damages and termination rights. Pittsburg Pepsi therefore was not the only party able to recover for breach.

Nor did the contracts express intent to give other bottlers their own enforcement right. The established practice was to report encroachment to PepsiCo for enforcement, which Pittsburg Pepsi repeatedly did. Territorial advantage was incidental for this enforcement question. The court affirmed summary judgment for Bottling Group on third-party-beneficiary rights while preserving Pittsburg Pepsi’s own contract claim against PepsiCo.

sections.title: Only the SEK business-interference theory proceeds to trial
sections.cue: Follow the tort distinctions and final remand.
paragraphs: Kansas business-interference law required probable advantage, knowledge, but-for causation, intentional misconduct, and damage, with malice meaning evil-mindedness or specific intent to injure. Bottling Group’s SEK dealings, resale quantities, complaints, and disputed knowledge could support causation and intentional interference. The court reversed that claim alone. PepsiCo’s broader creation of favorable conditions for outside purchasing did not establish direct interference or the necessary causal link to customers’ choices.

A distinct claim that Bottling Group induced PepsiCo to breach also failed. Even assuming it was not waived, there was no evidence of that direction of inducement; Pittsburg Pepsi’s account instead described PepsiCo encouraging Bottling Group.

PepsiCo had not consciously undertaken fiduciary obligations beyond the arm’s-length relationship. Franchise discretion and trust in fair dealing were insufficient, particularly with Pittsburg Pepsi’s independent pricing and information practices. This was a prediction of Kansas law, not application of a controlling state case on this precise relationship. Conspiracy required an actionable underlying wrong and multiple participants. With no actionable PepsiCo tort established, that theory failed against both defendants.

On December 20, 2005, the unanimous panel reversed for proceedings on reasonable territorial protection against PepsiCo and SEK interference against Bottling Group, affirmed the other rulings, and remanded. It awarded no damages and found neither defendant finally liable.
